title: The secret side of YouTube
content:
To unlock more of my reporting on how the internet is reshaping politics, business, media, and culture, and to read my deep dives into emerging online spaces and internet trends, become a paid subscriber today!

I cannot produce this newsletter without your financial support. Your money goes directly towards reporting costs.

When most people think of YouTube they picture hyper-saturated, attention-grabbing, MrBeast-style videos, professionally produced multi-cam podcasts, captivating scripted series and an endless library of television clips and music videos. Over the past 20 years, YouTube has undeniably succeeded in its goal to subsume traditional entertainment and become the “new Hollywood.” It is the number one streaming service in America and delivers entertainment and information to billions around the world.

But there’s another side of YouTube, that the vast majority of users never see.

On this secret side of YouTube, the app isn’t a polished entertainment platform, it’s a critical tool for self expression and a crucial pillar in our online communication infrastructure. To see this side of YouTube, you need to peek under the platform’s hood. You must subvert its many algorithms, recommendation systems, and features aimed at optimizing content for attention.

In this world, an anonymous man is playing the accordion to an audience of no one, a lonely goldfish swims alone in its tank, a family celebrates some sort of special occasion, a man surveys a parking lot full of trailers, cartoon noises play against a blank backdrop, or a town in Asia celebrates the new year. According to YouTube, every single one of these videos was not viewed by a single person before me.

I discovered these videos through a website called Astronaut.io, which was created back in 2017 by engineers Andrew Wong and James Thompson. It loops YouTube videos with little to no views at random, creating a never ending stream of mundane, intimate, and often never before seen moments in strangers’ lives.

There have been similar efforts to surface YouTube’s least-viewed content by gathering videos whose titles begin with the phrase IMG, the default naming convention attached to videos uploaded via iPhone back in 2009 to 2012. After making it easier for people to upload videos directly from their phones, YouTube reported a 1700% increase in total video uploads during the first half of 2009 alone.

The blog Ben Mini offers one catalog of this old, forgotten content. Another technologist made a bot that crawled YouTube and inventoried 5 million of these videos.

Recently, a group of researchers built a new tool with much greater ability to plunge the depths of secret YouTube. Thomas Germain, a journalist at the BBC, got access to the tool and spent weeks delving into “one of the first truly random samples of YouTube ever collected outside the company.”

“I saw a side of the internet that sometimes feels lost, one full of pure, unvarnished self-expression,” he writes. “It's an entire world that YouTube's all-seeing algorithm won't show you.”

He describes one video where “a man points the camera out of his bedroom window as a flurry breaks out in the dead of winter. ‘Here it is,’ he says. ‘The falling snow.’ The sound of a TV plays in the background. A bird lands on a nearby fence. 19 minutes go by. Nothing happens.’”

"The conversations we're having about YouTube are based on an impoverished view of what the platform really is," Ryan McGrady, the senior researcher on the project told the BBC. "When we just focus on what's popular, we miss how the vast majority of people actually use YouTube as uploaders, and overlooking the role it plays in our society."

"YouTube isn't just a vehicle for professionals," McGrady added. "We rely on it as the default video arm of the internet. YouTube is infrastructure. It's a critical tool that regular people use to communicate."

Share

To explore this hidden side of YouTube McGrady and his colleagues built a tool that serves up videos at random by scraping potential URLs. They then analyzed thousands of random videos to produce some fascinating insights about the platform.

For instance, the median YouTube video has been watched just 41 times and posts with more than 130 views are in the top third of the service's most popular content. As Germain notes, “the vast majority of YouTube is practically invisible.”

Germain’s piece, grapples with what these videos tell us about the platform and our deeply human desire for connection and self expression. He spoke to some of the people who uploaded these obscure videos about why they chose to post benign snippets of their lives to an app with billions of users.

"We tend to assume the reason to use social media is to try to be an influencer, either you're Joe Rogan or you're a failure. But that's the wrong way to think about it," Ethan Zuckerman, who leads the YouTube research as the director of the University of Massachusetts' Initiative for Digital Public Infrastructure, told the BBC.

Germain writes:

This stuff is bland enough to melt your brain. A bride gets ready for a photo shoot. A grouchy Korean man rants about politics. Six seconds of a martial arts instructor, devoid of context. Dash camera footage from a car struggling to escape a parking lot… Endless, mundane screen recordings of video games – the University of Massachusetts Amhurst study found people playing video games seems to make up almost 20% of YouTube.

Occasionally, you stumble on something fun, or more often, just plain weird. Three men performatively slapping each other's rear ends to a James Brown song. A woman reviews a brand of pre-sliced bologna (it's "not too bad")…

"The internet is deeply troubled, and we can't ignore the way tech companies are exacerbating those problems," McGrady says. "What makes me hopeful is that when you find a way to look at how people are really using the web, a lot of it still feels like the early internet. It's expression, communication, connection. Fundamentally, it's a place where regular people share themselves and do wonderful things."

The YouTube we talk about – the one full of celebrities, scandals and manufactured virality – only tells part of the story. The majority exists in quiet moments, in shaky camera work and voices meant for no one in particular. I watched hundreds of these videos. Everything one of them is public, but it's also clear that most people didn't upload this content for strangers. It was like being let in on a secret, a sprawling, uncurated documentary of human life.

As our country ventures further into a moral panic about the impacts of social media on our lives and mental health, bad actors pushing pseudoscience with best selling books continue to do endless media tours about why we must log off and disconnect. There is a concerted effort to sell people, especially young people, on the idea that the internet was a mistake, and we must all retreat back into a top-down media environment where information and free expression are restricted by those in power.

I think this is a huge mistake. The beauty of the internet is in its ability to connect people, and I think projects like this, that use technology to give a window into our shared humanity, are essential in remembering what the internet could be.

They reveal the way profit-driven incentives have warped these platforms, but also serve as a reminder of what technology could do. They show how technology can offer a window into other people’s worlds and broaden our understanding of our own lives. I think the best products and accounts online do these things.

After going down a hidden YouTube rabbit hole, I was reminded of my all-time favorite account on Instagram, Crisis Acting.

The page posts haphazard carousels of random videos from around the world, calling itself “THE PSYCHIC MAP OF RIGHT NOW.”

crisis.acting
A post shared by @crisis.acting

Much has been written about the current loneliness epidemic, and I think the reason people gravitate towards accounts like Crisis Acting or projects that resurface random old YouTube videos is because, there’s something about them that reaffirms our commonalities. They show how vast the world is, but also make us feel closer to each other. I love to read the comments on Crisis Acting videos, where people reveal the ways different video clips affected them or stirred up a memory.

Sad YouTube

In the fall of 2012, film director Mark Slutsky started a project called Sad YouTube, where he documented “moments of melancholy, sadness and saudade from the lives of strangers, gleaned from the unfairly maligned ocean of YouTube comments.”

For years, he catalogued YouTube comments and the videos they were attached to. “I wanted somewhere to preserve all of the wonderful, heartbreaking stories that seemed to be littered throughout YouTube’s comment section, unrecognized,” he wrote.

A couple years later, he wrote about the project for BuzzFeed News (RIP), saying: “The YouTube comment section has long been considered the worst place on the internet. You won't find much consensus about anything online, but one thing pretty much everyone can agree on — including, seemingly, the people at YouTube itself — is that the user-generated content beneath practically every video is a semi-literate cesspool. But for the last year I've been increasingly discovering… that everyone was wrong.”

He explains how the YouTube comment section had inadvertently “become the strangest and most wonderful place on the internet. A place that was fascinating, endlessly moving, and heartbreakingly human.”

“Dig deep into comments — particularly on pop songs — and you'll see that buried beneath the hate speech, the poorly formulated insults, and the Obama conspiracy theories are countless amazing nuggets of humanity,” he writes. “You'll find stories of love and loss, perfectly crystallized moments of nostalgia and saudade (a Portuguese word meaning an ineffable longing for something lost in time). It's a repository of memories, stories, and dreams, an accidental oral history of American life over the last 50 years written by the site's millions of visitors every day.”

It’s wild how prescient what Mark wrote over a decade ago is today, and how well his piece predicts what would ultimately happen to the internet. He talks about how in YouTube and Google’s quest to build a global product to maximize shareholder value, they unintentionally created this fantastic archive of humanity.

“Google seems totally unaware of the human and narrative gold mine it possesses in YouTube's comments section,” he writes, “and I fear it will just get rid of it altogether one day like it did Google Reader, Google Wave, or a million other projects whose uses weren't obvious.”

In January of 2014, Mark gave a talk about Sad YouTube at tech journalist Adrian Chen’s IRL Club, an event series for internet users in Brooklyn in the early 2010s. I remember crowding into the back of Baby's All Right in Williamsburg to see his talk live, and I really recommend watching it.

It’s a talk I have thought about so frequently over the years while writing about the internet:

The internet can be a bleak and miserable place, especially lately. But I hope that as it all inevitably becomes even more corporatized and profit-driven, we can find spaces or accounts online offer us an escape. It’s through these projects that we realize how inextricably interconnected we’ve become thanks to the internet.

As I wrote in my book Extremely Online, which documents the two and a half decade-long rise of the attention economy, while big tech has consolidated power, often against the individual, preying on your privacy, content, and attention, we should heed the lessons of the first twenty years of online life, and reflect those learnings in our work to build a better internet. We all want our existence validated, and increasingly, an online presence is the measure of that validation.
